impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which had been found willfully infringed by Eli Lilly. The court reinstated the jury verdict of infringement and invalidity defenses failure, remanding for further proceedings. This decision preserves patent protection for a major biologic drug category (anti-CGRP antibodies for headache treatment).
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that patent holders in the biologics space can obtain broad genus claims covering humanized antibodies without needing to disclose every possible species, so long as the specification provides sufficient guidance and the prior art supports the breadth of claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors like Eli Lilly face renewed infringement liability and potential enhanced damages for willful infringement of biologic method-of-treatment patents with broad functional claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Ingevity's conditioning of patent licenses on exclusive purchase of its unpatented carbon honeycomb products constituted unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the honeycombs were 'nonstaple goods' exempt from antitrust liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding Ingevity liable for unlawful tying under federal antitrust law. Ingevity had conditioned licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of its unpatented honeycomb products. The court rejected Ingevity's defense that its honeycombs were nonstaple goods lacking substantial non-infringing uses, affirming the damages award.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for companies defending against patent-based tying claims: if a patented product has substantial non-infringing uses, patent holders cannot leverage patent licenses to coerce purchase of unpatented goods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who bundle patent licenses with requirements to purchase unpatented supplies or components face significant antitrust liability, including treble damages, if the tied product has substantial non-infringing uses.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and a model of function calls are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages for patent infringement may include foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, finding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents (covering malware detection via emulation and comparison to behavioral models) are abstract at Alice step one, requiring remand for step two analysis. The court also held that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing software-related patents gain a stronger basis for challenging claims as abstract under § 101, and the ruling limits damages exposure from foreign product sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the cybersecurity and software space face heightened risk that their claims will be found abstract, and cannot easily recover damages based on the accused infringer's worldwide revenue.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content specifications to a wireless device's screen size and capabilities before delivery are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held on cross-appeal that GoTV's patent claims covering server-side content tailoring for wireless devices are ineligible under § 101, reversing the jury's $2.5 million infringement verdict for Netflix. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content to a device's capabilities, requiring entry of judgment for Netflix.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming and technology companies gain protection against infringement claims based on broad software method patents covering routine content adaptation functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting claims covering server-side optimization of content delivery face significant § 101 eligibility challenges, potentially rendering their patents unenforceable.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that the plaintiff established protectable trade secrets under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the underlying concepts were generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, holding that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting verdict was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a reinforced requirement that plaintiffs must clearly demonstrate their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for competitive advantage must ensure robust documentation showing that their asserted secrets go beyond publicly available or generally known information, or risk losing protection.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was proper on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim alleging attempted monopolization through a fraudulently obtained patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment for both parties, finding genuine disputes of material fact precluded resolution on both Tenaris's inequitable conduct in obtaining coiled tubing patents and Global Tubing's Walker Process antitrust claim. The court remanded for trial on whether Tenaris committed fraud on the patent office and whether that fraud supported an attempted monopolization claim.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against inequitable conduct allegations benefit from the court's insistence on factual development before such serious charges can be resolved, preserving their right to trial.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face continued exposure to both inequitable conduct defenses and treble-damage Walker Process antitrust claims when prior art disclosure during prosecution is questioned, creating significant litigation risk.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent infringement claims for multicore processor core-selection technology are barred by extraterritoriality when the accused products are designed in the U.S. but manufactured and initially deployed abroad, and whether the district court properly struck plaintiff's damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent on extraterritoriality grounds, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether sufficient infringing acts occurred domestically. The court also reversed the striking of VLSI's damages theories, remanding for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against products designed domestically but manufactured abroad gain broader ability to pursue infringement claims, as the court recognizes that U.S.-based design and testing activities may support domestic infringement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing operations face greater infringement exposure for products designed or tested in the U.S., even when final assembly and initial deployment occur abroad.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside of personal knowledge at summary judgment, and whether source code constitutes hearsay, in the context of the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative's deposition testimony is admissible even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of historical events, and that computer source code (as opposed to human-readable comments within it) is not hearsay. This significantly impacts how prior art sales evidence may be proven.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded evidentiary tools to prove on-sale bar invalidity: corporate representative testimony need not be based on personal knowledge, and source code is admissible as non-hearsay to show prior art functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges, as opponents can use corporate designees with no firsthand knowledge and source code evidence to establish pre-critical-date commercial activity.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims covering non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility for some asserted claims while affirming eligibility for others, creating a split outcome on § 101 for communication technology patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, including upholding the damages expert testimony. This case provides guidance on § 101 eligibility for claims at the boundary between abstract mathematical concepts and practical communication technology implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communication standards technology may sustain eligibility for claims that incorporate specific technical implementations beyond abstract mathematical optimization, preserving enforcement options against standard-essential patent infringers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued uncertainty as § 101 eligibility determinations may vary claim-by-claim within the same patent family, complicating licensing and litigation strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen functionality violated § 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated § 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement devices, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing models. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with established domestic industries can effectively use ITC exclusion orders to block importation of infringing consumer electronics, providing a powerful enforcement mechanism beyond district court litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant commercial disruption from ITC exclusion orders that can block importation of popular consumer products, creating urgency to design around patented features or obtain licenses.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly denied Polygroup's motion for JMOL of obviousness and for a new trial on damages for Willis's pre-lit artificial tree patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of JMOL of obviousness and motion for new trial on damages, upholding the jury's infringement verdict for Willis's patent on pre-lit artificial trees with integrated mechanical and electrical connections. The decision reinforces the standard for overcoming a jury's non-obviousness finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's deference to jury findings on non-obviousness, making it difficult for accused infringers to overturn validity determinations post-trial.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a damages remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft, finding the district court applied an overly restrictive standard to the expert's methodology. The court held that a patent plaintiff cannot be denied access to trial solely because a damages expert report was improperly excluded, and remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that Daubert challenges will effectively end patent cases at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent cases face reduced ability to obtain summary judgment through Daubert exclusion of damages experts, potentially increasing litigation costs and trial exposure.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled district court declaratory judgment action when it missed the deadline for seeking a stay in a previously filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling the declaratory judgment action. This prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate filing deadlines to obtain mandatory stays of parallel district court proceedings through strategic dismissal and refiling.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action cannot cure the missed deadline by refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including approval of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that PACER fees exceeded statutory authority by funding expenses unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld attorneys' fees awards, incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, and the settlement's distribution plan providing full or substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users.
impacts.positiveImplications: The decision validates incentive awards to organizational class representatives and confirms that the Little Tucker Act provides district court jurisdiction for fee overcharge claims, supporting future class actions challenging excessive government fees.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Board regarding discretionary denial of inter partes review institution constitute a 'general statement of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's Fintiv and other instructions governing discretionary IPR non-institution decisions are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA § 553(b). The court emphasized that the Director retains unreviewable discretion over institution decisions and the instructions do not bind the Director.
impacts.positiveImplications: The PTO retains broad flexibility to issue and modify guidance on IPR institution without formal rulemaking, allowing rapid policy adjustments that may benefit patent holders by limiting IPR institution in cases with parallel district court litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies and other frequent IPR petitioners cannot force formal rulemaking for IPR institution policies, limiting their ability to challenge discretionary non-institution decisions that reduce opportunities to challenge patents administratively.
